prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a single, well-defined invention with a concrete before-and-after. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes Doppler, recoil and lattice-induced shifts while many atoms are interrogated in parallel, and that is what took optical clocks from the 1e-15 regime to below 1e-18. The result is a change in what can be measured and how accurately. It feeds directly into the prospective redefinition of the SI second, relativistic geodesy, searches for varying constants and many-body clock physics. The performance has been reproduced and surpassed in independent laboratories with Sr, Yb and Hg, with routine international comparisons, so the physics is stable and the maturity question is largely settled. The attribution is the cleanest on the list: Katori for the concept and the first lattice clock, Ye for pushing it to record accuracy and coherence and for tying it to frequency-comb and ultrastable-laser technology. A two-person prize needs no arbitrary cut.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is precedent and framing. The 2005 prize (Hall and Hansch, comb-based optical frequency metrology) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, ion control, which includes the Al+ optical clock) already honoured the neighbouring ingredients, so a clock prize must be framed around the lattice concept rather than optical clocks generally. A second reservation is timing: the redefinition of the second is still pending, so one could argue for waiting. Finally, ion-clock groups and the broader ecosystem of comb and laser-stabilisation contributors sit outside the two names, and I know the field is crowded enough that a narrowly worded citation will be tested.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, as the original transfer of cavity-QED ideas to a chip and the architecture of essentially all superconducting quantum processors, with a natural theory-plus-two-experiments trio.
responses.response: I agree that circuit QED is original and well confirmed, and I ranked it third myself. My reservation is the 2025 prize to Clarke, Devoret and Martinis for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which is close enough that the Academy would have to explain what is new. The credit also overlaps with Devoret, Girvin and the Yale transmon work, so the trio is more contestable than the lattice clock pair. I do not think the 2025 overlap is disqualifying, which is why I keep it as an alternative. But I rank it below the clock because the clock has no recent neighbouring prize and a cleaner two-person attribution.

responses.point: Olsson ranks spherical-aberration correction first, as an invention with a concrete before-and-after that brought routine sub-angstrom imaging to materials physics, with Rose, Haider and Urban as the natural trio.
responses.response: I accept that this is a genuine invention, mature and commercially routine, and the roles of Rose, Haider and Urban are well separated. Where I differ is on how it ranks against the clock. Both are instrument-driven advances with broad downstream use, but the lattice clock changes the limit on a fundamental measured quantity, frequency, and enables tests of constants and relativity. The corrector improves a tool for physics and materials science. I also note that Krivanek's STEM correction work, which you flag, leaves a real attribution gap. I would not oppose a combined configuration if the committee wanted two parts, but I do not see it as stronger than the clock on its own.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the lattice clock fifth. He regards it as a clean and important instrumentation advance with a fair two-person allocation, but he notes that the ion-clock groups and the Hall/Hansch precedent affect the framing, and he puts twisted bilayer graphene first.
responses.response: The framing point is fair and I share it, so the citation should stay on the lattice concept. I do not think precedent weakens the case: the 2005 prize rewarded comb-based frequency measurement, while the lattice clock is a different idea about how to trap and interrogate the atoms. On twisted bilayer graphene I accept the originality and the quality of the prediction-to-experiment story, but you and others note that the origin of the superconductivity is still debated and that Cao and others are outside the credited names. I read the clock as more mature and with less attribution risk, so I would not move it below the graphene candidate.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs experimental discovery first as an overdue, clearly specified discovery, but concedes that the choice of three among four collaboration leaders is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree the discovery is not in doubt and was confirmed by two experiments. My difficulty is the same one you name: the credit is carried by thousands of people, and any three of Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee is an arbitrary cut. Olsson reached a different three-name subset from yours, which suggests the committee cannot settle it. A prize whose recipients can be defended only by an institutional choice is weaker than one where the inventors are identifiable by their papers. I have not looked at this from a particle physics perspective in detail, so I would defer to you on how the committee has handled collaborations before, but on the evidence here I rank the clock higher.

uncertainties: Whether the pending redefinition of the SI second should be treated as a reason for timing or as an argument to wait.
How narrowly the citation must be worded so that it is clearly distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Whether the committee would prefer a two-part prize pairing the clock with a quantum-information or instrument candidate; I have not seen a combination that is stronger than the clock alone.
How much the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits should weigh against circuit QED, which is my first alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. A documented tangential connection is my research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall's 2005 prize is part of the precedent for this field. My profile records no collaboration with either candidate. My own work on laser spectroscopy and ultrastable-laser-related stabilisation is in the same technical area, so the committee may want to be aware of that proximity.
